title: The Receptor Makes a Round Trip

scenes.tts: Cells from one patient carry receptors that grip L D L normally. Yet the L D L stays outside the cell. A receptor has to do more than bind. It must be gathered into the right patch of membrane, carried inside, let go of its cargo, and come back.
scenes.caption: Cells from one patient carry receptors that grip LDL normally. Yet the LDL stays outside the cell. A receptor has to do more than bind. It must be gathered into the right patch of membrane, carried inside, let go of its cargo, and come back.
scenes.visual: Receptors on a membrane hold LDL; a crossed-out arrow shows LDL not entering; receptors gather and five step chips light in turn
scenes.narration: Cells from one patient carry receptors that grip LDL normally. Yet the LDL stays outside the cell. A receptor has to do more than bind. It must be gathered into the right patch of membrane, carried inside, let go of its cargo, and come back.

scenes.tts: In mammalian cells, the steps run in order. Clathrin builds the coat, but clathrin binds neither membrane nor cargo. Adaptors do that. An adaptor called A P 2 binds a lipid in the inner leaflet of the membrane. Adaptors also read short sorting motifs in cargo tails. Then they recruit clathrin. The lattice grows, and the membrane curves into a pit. Dynamin forms a collar around the narrow neck. Using G T P, it drives the membrane to split. A chaperone then pulls the lattice apart.

scenes.tts: The uncoated vesicle fuses with an early endosome. Its lumen is mildly acid, roughly p H 6. For L D L, acid is the sorting signal. At this p H, L D L comes off its receptor. Receptor and cargo now part.
scenes.caption: The uncoated vesicle fuses with an early endosome. Its lumen is mildly acid, roughly pH 6. For LDL, acid is the sorting signal. At this pH, LDL comes off its receptor. Receptor and cargo now part.
scenes.visual: Vesicle merges into an early endosome; lumen tints acid; LDL lifts off the receptors into the lumen
scenes.narration: The uncoated vesicle fuses with an early endosome. Its lumen is mildly acid, roughly pH 6. For LDL, acid is the sorting signal. At this pH, LDL comes off its receptor. Receptor and cargo now part.

scenes.tts: The receptor goes back. Empty receptors collect in narrow tubules that pinch off and return to the plasma membrane. The L D L stays in the lumen. In human A431 cells, Rab5 was replaced by Rab7 on single endosomes carrying L D L. The authors read this as the compartment maturing. The L D L goes on to the lysosome. There, enzymes digest it and release cholesterol.

scenes.tts: These numbers are made up for practice. Cells bind labeled L D L in the cold, where nothing enters. Then they warm up, and a wash strips the surface. Normal cells bound 40 and took in 30. That is 75 percent. Strain X bound only one point zero, which is two point five percent of normal. That is a binding defect. Strain Y bound 38 but took in just 3. That is seven point nine percent. That is an entry defect.
scenes.caption: These numbers are made up for practice. Cells bind labeled LDL in the cold, where nothing enters. Then they warm up, and a wash strips the surface. That is an entry defect.

scenes.tts: So the receptor makes a round trip. It binds at the surface, enters in a coated vesicle, lets go of L D L in the acid endosome, and returns. The L D L travels one way, to the lysosome. Different mutations break different steps, so a patient's cells can show which step failed. Keep this rule. A receptor must bind, enter, release, and return.
